newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Killers of U.S. student seek amnesty in S.Africa.
newsitem.headline: Killers of U.S. student seek amnesty in S.Africa.

text.p: The parents of a U.S. student murdered by a South African mob said on Tuesday they had no objection to her killers obtaining amnesty from the country's Truth and Reconciliation Commission.

"We want simply for people to understand that we're supportive of the process, but that in the end it's really up to the community of South Africa to forgive its own," said Peter Biehl, father of 26-year-old Californian Amy Biehl who was murdered in 1993.
Four black youths were convicted of murdering her in Guguletu township outside Cape Town and were each sentenced to 18 years in jail.

The four -- Mzikhona Nofemela, Ntobeko Peni, Vusumzi Ntamo and Mongezi Manqina -- are due to appear before Archbishop Desmond Tutu's truth commission later on Tuesday to apply for amnesty for what they say was a political crime.
Biehl had come to South Africa as an exchange student and was dropping off black friends in Guguletu when a mob stopped her car, dragged her from it and beat, stabbed and stoned her to death.
"If amnesty is granted, then we're certainly not going to oppose it, and we don't oppose it going in," said Peter Biehl, who travelled to South Africa with his wife Linda to attend the hearing.
"She knew what she was doing, she was doing what she wanted to do," he said. "We're excited to be bound here forever, and we are here forever...Amy made sure of that."
Linda Biehl said she hoped the four youths would not commit further acts of violence if they were released.

"We want to make sure that if amnesty is granted, that these young men have skills to enable them to return to society and that they don't become criminals or there's not more violence associated with them," she said.
"We want South Africa to go forward. That's why Amy was working here."
The four men applying for amnesty on Tuesday were members of the black radical Pan Africanist Congress, which fought apartheid under the slogan "one settler, one bullet".
The group won less that two percent of the vote in South Africa's first all-race election in 1994.

The truth commission was set up in 1995 to investigate human rights abuses by all sides during apartheid, with the aim of healing pyschological wounds. It has powers to absolve perpetrators who make full confessions.
